text:
Sleep loss harms memory at both ends of the process. After one sleepless night, Matthew Walker's group found, the hippocampus can encode about 40% less new information. It is like an inbox nobody has emptied, so it can't take more.

The deeper damage happens offline. During slow-wave sleep, three kinds of activity occur together: slow oscillations at 0.5–1 Hz, spindles at 11–16 Hz, and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples. Together they replay the day's memory traces and send them to the neocortex for long-term storage. If you skip that night shift, consolidation stalls.

Researchers also suspect that the glymphatic system, which clears waste from the brain, falls behind. In mice, its channels between cells widen by about 60% during sleep. Without that clearing, metabolic debris such as amyloid-beta may cloud the next day's learning.

Even a partial shortfall adds up. Subjects limited to six hours of sleep for two weeks did as poorly on attention tests as people who had gone without sleep entirely, yet they rated themselves as only mildly impaired.

In short, memory is built by day but stored at night.
